title: Handbook close
hookLine: fifty-three chapters in fifty-six days; the handbook is now yours to carry

cards: Fifty-three short sections in fifty-six days. That's the handbook, read in order, start to finish.
Eight weeks ago it opened with Arrian, the student who boiled his teacher's lessons down into a little book meant to be kept in the hand.
The Greek name, enchiridion, means just that: the thing in the hand, a word also used for a small knife. Today it closes. Not to go on a shelf.
A handbook on a shelf has missed its whole point.

teach.h: FIRST: WHAT IS UP TO US.
teach.b: Section one split the world into two piles: what is up to us, our judgments, desires and choices, and what isn't, our body, property, reputation and office.
The line was start here, and almost everything after flowed from that one sort. Section five gave its sharpest form: people are disturbed not by things, but by their judgments about things.

teach.h: TOOLS: THE JUG, THE BATHS, THE BANQUET.
teach.b: Then the everyday tools. The jug you love is a jug. The baths will have splashing and shoving, so keep your purpose.
When the dish comes around, take a modest share. You're an actor in a play; play your part well. The insult only harms through your judgment.
Then living with other people. What the role asks. Mostly quiet.
Yes means yes. Ask, don't tell. He missed the rest.
The table matters. It seemed right to him. Two handles.
Quickly, not badly. These can be the hardest to keep, because they happen in conversation, fast, with no time to look anything up.

teach.h: THE ROAD: BLAME NO ONE. WILLINGLY.
teach.b: And the road: signs of progress, starting with blame no one. Live the book, not just explain it. How long will you wait?
And at the very end, Cleanthes: lead me on, and I'll follow willingly.
Arrian made this book to be carried, and no one carries fifty-three things. So the last practice is a choice: three lines to keep in the hand.
Tomorrow a new part of the path begins: the Discourses, the longer record of Epictetus actually teaching, joking and scolding in his classroom.

how: Many people who study the Enchiridion keep a few favorite sections written on a card or in a notebook and return to them daily, as Arrian intended the book to be kept at hand.

o: a handbook: the thing kept in the hand
a scroll of laws read aloud in court
a collection of prayers to the Greek gods

s: enchiridion means a thing kept in the hand
Arrian made it to be carried, not shelved.
the handbook ends with a summary of Stoic doctrine
it ends with four old sayings, from Cleanthes, Euripides and Socrates.
the Discourses are a longer record of Epictetus teaching
that's the next part of the path.

games.q: you've finished the handbook. what did Arrian make it for?
o: to sit on a shelf as a classic.
to be kept in the hand, ready for use.
to be memorized for an exam.
games.why: enchiridion: the thing in the hand. no one carries fifty-three things, so choose three.

practice: Let the eight weeks drift by: the two piles, the jug, the actor, the raven, the cup, the role, the quiet, the handles, the wool, the contest, the hymn.
Don't chase any of them; just notice which three keep coming back on their own, and say each one quietly, once. If you like, write them on something small enough to carry.

wordCard.voice: Enchiridion. The Greek name for the handbook, meaning the thing in the hand; fifty-three sections in fifty-six days, made to be carried, not shelved. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: something in the hand, a handbook, or a small dagger kept close.

carryVoice: Your line: carry three. A handbook belongs in the hand, not on the shelf. Day three hundred eighty-seven.
